_comment: The SECOND disease, and the proof of the architecture. Almost nothing here is a skill: the pathway is references to the same core and respiratory skills COPD uses, with the OPPOSITE emphasis at every step. Percussion is one authored skill; COPD says expect hyperresonance and this file says expect stony dullness. That contrast is also the best way to teach both.
name: Pleural effusion
oneLine: Fluid in the pleural space, and the question of why it is there

chapters.title: Basics
chapters.blurb: What it is, and why the cause matters more than the fluid

chapters.title: Approach to the patient
chapters.blurb: Identical to every other bedside encounter

chapters.title: History
chapters.blurb: The same questions, pointing somewhere else

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: Expect a shorter history than COPD: breathlessness over days to weeks rather than years, often with pleuritic chest pain that eases as the fluid accumulates and separates the pleural surfaces.

skill.hx.resp.dyspnea.expect: Expect breathlessness that is progressive but recent, and often positional. Ask specifically about pleuritic pain, fever, weight loss and night sweats, because in India tuberculosis is a leading cause and malignancy is the other.

skill.hx.resp.cough_sputum.expect: Cough is usually dry and non-productive here, which is itself a point against COPD and chronic bronchitis. Haemoptysis raises malignancy, tuberculosis and infarction.

chapters.title: General examination
chapters.blurb: Looking for the cause, not the fluid

skill.gen.clubbing.expect: Unlike COPD, clubbing here is INFORMATIVE rather than a red flag against the diagnosis. It points to the underlying cause: bronchial carcinoma, empyema, bronchiectasis or mesothelioma.

skill.gen.edema.expect: Bilateral oedema with a raised JVP suggests the effusion is a TRANSUDATE from heart failure, which changes the whole workup. Look also for the stigmata of chronic liver disease and for the puffiness of nephrotic syndrome.

skill.gen.appearance.expect: Look for cachexia and lymphadenopathy, which point to malignancy or tuberculosis, and for the position the patient adopts: many lie on the side of the effusion, which splints it and lets the good lung expand.

chapters.title: Respiratory examination
chapters.blurb: The same seven skills, every one of them the opposite of COPD

skill.exam.resp.inspection.expect: Expect a fuller, less mobile hemithorax on the affected side, with reduced movement there. Not the barrel chest of COPD: the asymmetry is the finding.

skill.exam.resp.trachea.expect: A large effusion PUSHES the mediastinum AWAY from the affected side. If the trachea is pulled TOWARDS a dull hemithorax, this is not a simple effusion: think collapse behind an obstructing lesion, or a fibrothorax.

skill.exam.resp.expansion.expect: Expect ASYMMETRICAL reduction, with the affected side lagging. This is the finding COPD never gives you, and it is why the floating-thumb technique matters.

skill.exam.resp.percussion.expect: STONY dullness over the fluid, the most characteristic sign. Compare it with the hyperresonance of COPD: the same manoeuvre, the opposite note. The upper level is classically higher in the axilla than in front or behind.

skill.exam.resp.auscultation.expect: Breath sounds are ABSENT or greatly reduced over the fluid, with normal sounds above. Bronchial breathing may be heard just above the fluid level, where compressed lung conducts sound.

skill.exam.resp.added_sounds.expect: Usually none over the fluid. A pleural rub may be heard early, before much fluid has collected, and disappears as the surfaces separate. That disappearance is a sign, not an improvement.

skill.exam.resp.vocal_resonance.expect: Reduced over the fluid. Completing the triad matters here: stony dullness plus absent breath sounds plus reduced vocal resonance IS the effusion, and any one of them alone is not.

chapters.blurb: The triad, and what changes it

stations.title: Examine the respiratory system
stations.task: This 44-year-old woman has been breathless for three weeks. Examine her respiratory system and present your findings.
examinerQuestions: Which way is the trachea deviated, and what would it mean if it were deviated the other way?
Give me the triad you found and what it localises.
How would you decide whether this is a transudate or an exudate?

skill.effusion.basics.title: What a pleural effusion is
skill.effusion.basics.oneLine: Fluid in a space that normally holds a few millilitres
skill.effusion.basics.why: A pleural effusion is never a diagnosis on its own, it is a finding with a cause, and the entire clinical task is finding that cause. Students who stop at 'pleural effusion' have answered half the question.
skill.effusion.basics.body: The pleural space normally contains only about 10 to 20 mL of fluid, continuously produced and reabsorbed. An effusion is an excess, arising when formation exceeds absorption.
keyPoints: A pleural effusion is a SIGN, not a diagnosis. The question is always why the fluid is there.
The first division is transudate versus exudate, because it splits the causes into two very different lists.
A transudate arises from altered hydrostatic or oncotic pressure with normal pleural membranes: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia.
An exudate arises from an inflamed or diseased pleura leaking protein: infection including tuberculosis, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, connective tissue disease, pancreatitis.
About 500 mL is usually needed before the effusion is detectable clinically, though blunting of the costophrenic angle appears on a chest radiograph at around 200 to 300 mL.
In India tuberculosis is a leading cause of a lymphocytic exudative effusion in a young adult, and malignancy in an older one.
pitfalls: Treating the effusion and never establishing the cause.
Assuming a small effusion in a patient with heart failure needs tapping, when a bilateral transudate consistent with the clinical picture often does not.
Forgetting that a unilateral effusion in a patient with heart failure, or one that fails to resolve with treatment, still needs investigating.

probes.q: How much fluid is normally in the pleural space?
probes.a: About 10 to 20 mL.

probes.q: What is the first and most useful division of the causes?
probes.a: Transudate versus exudate.

probes.q: Name three causes of a transudative effusion.
probes.a: Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia.

probes.q: Roughly how much fluid before an effusion is detectable clinically, and how much on a chest radiograph?
probes.a: Around 500 mL to be clinically detectable; blunting of the costophrenic angle at roughly 200 to 300 mL on a plain film.

probes.q: A patient with known heart failure has a UNILATERAL effusion that does not resolve with diuresis. What do you do?
probes.a: Investigate it rather than attributing it to the heart failure. A unilateral or non-resolving effusion needs a diagnostic tap to exclude infection, tuberculosis and malignancy, even when there is an obvious transudative explanation.

skill.effusion.signs.title: The effusion picture
skill.effusion.signs.oneLine: One triad, and the findings that mean it is not a simple effusion
skill.effusion.signs.why: Effusion is the cleanest example in the whole respiratory examination of why findings are read as a PATTERN rather than a list. Any one of the three signs has other causes; together they are close to diagnostic, and their combination localises the problem to the pleural space rather than the lung.
skill.effusion.signs.body: Over the fluid: stony dull percussion note, absent or greatly reduced breath sounds, and reduced vocal resonance. Everything else follows from the volume of fluid and from what caused it.
keyPoints: THE TRIAD: stony dullness, absent breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance, all over the same area.
Reduced expansion on the affected side, and a fuller, less mobile hemithorax.
Mediastinal shift AWAY from the effusion when it is large. The trachea and the apex beat should agree with each other.
Bronchial breathing may appear just ABOVE the fluid level, where lung is compressed but still aerated and conducts sound.
A pleural rub may be present early and disappears as fluid separates the surfaces. Its disappearance is not improvement.
The upper border of dullness is classically highest in the axilla, following the curve of the fluid.

Findings that mean this is NOT a simple effusion: the trachea PULLED TOWARDS the dull side (collapse behind an obstructing lesion, or fibrothorax), or dullness with PRESERVED vocal resonance and bronchial breathing throughout (consolidation, not fluid).
pitfalls: Calling stony dullness alone an effusion. Consolidation, collapse and a raised hemidiaphragm are all dull.
Missing that the trachea is pulled towards rather than pushed away, which changes the diagnosis completely.
Reporting bronchial breathing over the fluid rather than above it, and so calling consolidation.
Examining the front only. A modest effusion is often easiest to find at the back, with the patient sitting forward.

probes.q: Give the triad of a pleural effusion.
probes.a: Stony dull percussion note, absent or reduced breath sounds, and reduced vocal resonance.

probes.q: Which way does the trachea deviate with a large effusion?
probes.a: Away from the side of the effusion.

probes.q: The trachea is pulled TOWARDS a stony dull hemithorax. What does that tell you?
probes.a: This is not a simple effusion. A pulling process is present: lung collapse, often behind an obstructing bronchial lesion, or a fibrothorax. It needs urgent imaging and usually bronchoscopy.

probes.q: Why can bronchial breathing be heard just above an effusion?
probes.a: Lung immediately above the fluid is compressed but still patent and aerated. Compressed lung conducts sound from the central airways better than normal aerated lung, so bronchial breathing appears at the upper border while sounds over the fluid itself are absent.

skill.effusion.differential.title: A dull base is not always fluid
skill.effusion.differential.oneLine: What else gives that note, and which cause is behind the fluid
skill.effusion.differential.why: There are two differentials here and students often answer only one. The first is what else produces a dull base; the second, and the important one, is what caused the effusion. Answering only the first leaves the patient undiagnosed.
skill.effusion.differential.body: Work the two questions in order: is this fluid, and if so, why is it there.
keyPoints: IS IT FLUID? Consolidation gives dullness but with INCREASED vocal resonance and bronchial breathing. Collapse gives dullness with the trachea pulled TOWARDS it. A raised hemidiaphragm and a pleural thickening or fibrothorax both give dullness with little else. Ultrasound settles it at the bedside.
WHY IS IT THERE, transudate: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia, peritoneal dialysis.

WHY IS IT THERE, exudate: parapneumonic effusion and empyema, TUBERCULOSIS, malignancy including mesothelioma, pulmonary embolism, connective tissue disease such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus, pancreatitis, subphrenic abscess.
In an Indian adult with a unilateral lymphocytic exudate, fever and weight loss, tuberculosis is the leading diagnosis until excluded.
A bloody effusion narrows things sharply: malignancy, pulmonary infarction, trauma. A frankly purulent one is an empyema and is a drainage emergency.
Pulmonary embolism can produce either a transudate or an exudate, and is the classic cause that gets missed because the effusion is small.
pitfalls: Stopping at 'pleural effusion' without naming a cause or a plan to find one.
Not considering tuberculosis in an endemic setting.
Attributing a unilateral effusion to heart failure without evidence, when heart failure effusions are usually bilateral or right-sided.
Forgetting embolism because the effusion is small and there is a more obvious explanation.

probes.q: How do you distinguish consolidation from effusion at the bedside?
probes.a: Both are dull, but consolidation gives INCREASED vocal resonance and bronchial breathing, while an effusion gives reduced vocal resonance and absent breath sounds.

probes.q: Name four exudative causes.
probes.a: Parapneumonic effusion and empyema, tuberculosis, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, connective tissue disease, pancreatitis.

probes.q: A 34-year-old with a unilateral lymphocytic exudate, three weeks of fever and weight loss. Most likely cause in India, and how would you pursue it?
probes.a: Tuberculous pleural effusion. Pursue it with pleural fluid adenosine deaminase, lymphocyte predominance, mycobacterial testing including Xpert MTB/RIF, and pleural biopsy where the diagnosis remains uncertain, since fluid culture alone has low yield.

skill.ix.effusion.imaging.title: Imaging the effusion
skill.ix.effusion.imaging.oneLine: The film shows it; ultrasound is what you actually use
skill.ix.effusion.imaging.why: Understanding what each modality can and cannot answer prevents the two commonest errors: calling a dense hemithorax an effusion without confirming fluid, and attempting a blind tap.
skill.ix.effusion.imaging.body: Plain film to detect, ultrasound to confirm and guide, CT to explain.
keyPoints: Chest radiograph: blunting of the costophrenic angle at roughly 200 to 300 mL, with the classic rising meniscus laterally. A completely opaque hemithorax with the mediastinum pushed AWAY is a massive effusion; pulled TOWARDS is collapse.
A lateral decubitus film can show whether the fluid layers freely, and so whether it is loculated, though ultrasound has largely replaced it.

ULTRASOUND is the practical test: it confirms fluid, estimates volume, shows septations and loculations, and marks the safe site. Ultrasound guidance for pleural procedures reduces complications and is the standard of care.
CT with contrast, ideally with fluid still present, characterises the pleura: nodular or circumferential thickening suggests malignancy or empyema, and it shows the underlying lung and mediastinum.
NEVER perform a blind tap based on a plain film alone.
pitfalls: Attempting aspiration without ultrasound, which is how iatrogenic pneumothorax and organ injury happen.
Reading an opaque hemithorax without checking which way the mediastinum has moved.
Draining all the fluid before CT, when pleural nodularity is easiest to see with fluid still there to outline it.

probes.q: Which imaging test should guide a pleural tap?
probes.a: Ultrasound.

probes.q: An opaque hemithorax with the trachea deviated away. What is it?
probes.a: A massive pleural effusion.

probes.q: Why is ultrasound better than a plain film here?
probes.a: It confirms that the opacity is fluid rather than solid, estimates the volume, shows septations and loculations that change management, and marks a safe puncture site in real time.

skill.ix.effusion.tap.title: Pleural aspiration and Light's criteria
skill.ix.effusion.tap.oneLine: The one test that answers why the fluid is there
skill.ix.effusion.tap.why: Everything before this narrows the possibilities; the tap decides. Light's criteria are worth knowing exactly, because they are highly sensitive for an exudate and misapplying them sends the whole workup down the wrong branch.
skill.ix.effusion.tap.body: A diagnostic aspiration under ultrasound guidance, sent for the tests that actually change management.
keyPoints: LIGHT'S CRITERIA: the fluid is an EXUDATE if ANY ONE of these holds. Pleural fluid protein divided by serum protein greater than 0.5. Pleural fluid LDH divided by serum LDH greater than 0.6. Pleural fluid LDH greater than two thirds of the upper limit of the normal serum LDH.
Send simultaneous SERUM protein and LDH, or the criteria cannot be applied at all. This is the commonest practical error.
Always send: protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cell count with differential, Gram stain and culture, cytology.
In a suspected tuberculous effusion add adenosine deaminase and mycobacterial testing including a nucleic acid amplification test, and note the lymphocyte predominance.

Light's criteria are very sensitive for exudates but misclassify some transudates, particularly in a patient already on diuretics. Where the clinical picture says transudate, a serum-to-pleural-fluid albumin gradient above 1.2 g/dL supports a transudate.
A low pH and low glucose in a parapneumonic effusion indicate a complicated effusion needing DRAINAGE, not just antibiotics.
Frank pus means empyema: drain it.
Cytology has a moderate yield in malignancy from a single sample, so a negative cytology does not exclude it. Repeat sampling or pleural biopsy may be needed.
pitfalls: Sending pleural fluid without simultaneous serum protein and LDH, making Light's criteria unusable.
Draining a large effusion too fast, risking re-expansion pulmonary oedema. Stop for chest tightness or persistent cough.
Taking a negative cytology as excluding malignancy.
Treating a complicated parapneumonic effusion with antibiotics alone when the pH and glucose say it needs a drain.

probes.q: State Light's criteria.
probes.a: Exudate if any one of: pleural/serum protein above 0.5; pleural/serum LDH above 0.6; pleural LDH above two thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

probes.q: What must you send alongside the pleural fluid?
probes.a: Simultaneous serum protein and LDH. Without them Light's criteria cannot be applied.

probes.q: Pleural fluid pH is low with a low glucose in a parapneumonic effusion. What does that change?
probes.a: It indicates a complicated parapneumonic effusion, which needs chest tube drainage in addition to antibiotics rather than antibiotics alone.

probes.q: The picture is clearly heart failure but Light's criteria call it an exudate. How do you resolve it?
probes.a: Light's criteria are very sensitive and misclassify some transudates, especially after diuresis. Calculate the serum-to-pleural-fluid albumin gradient: a value above 1.2 g/dL supports a transudate despite Light's. Treat the heart failure and reassess rather than launching an exudate workup.

skill.ix.effusion.tap.dosingNote: Thresholds and criteria only. Procedure technique, sedation and any drug must follow your current institutional protocol, and the procedure itself is performed under supervision. CliniX does not prescribe.

skill.tx.effusion.title: Managing the effusion
skill.tx.effusion.oneLine: Treat the cause; drain only what needs draining
skill.tx.effusion.why: The reflex to drain every effusion is wrong and occasionally harmful. Management divides cleanly by whether the fluid is a transudate, an uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion, a complicated one or an empyema, or malignant, and each takes a different path.
skill.tx.effusion.body: Decide what the fluid is, then act.
keyPoints: TRANSUDATE: treat the underlying cause. A heart-failure effusion usually resolves with treatment of the heart failure; drainage is for symptomatic relief only, and a non-resolving or unilateral one must be investigated.
UNCOMPLICATED PARAPNEUMONIC: antibiotics for the pneumonia and observation. No drain needed.

COMPLICATED PARAPNEUMONIC or EMPYEMA: chest tube drainage plus antibiotics. Delay causes a fibrothorax and a trapped lung. Intrapleural fibrinolytics or surgical decortication are considered where drainage fails.
TUBERCULOUS: standard antituberculosis therapy under the national programme. Most resolve without drainage; drain for symptoms or for a large effusion.

MALIGNANT: therapeutic aspiration for symptoms, then a definitive measure for recurrence, either pleurodesis or an indwelling pleural catheter, chosen with the patient and depending on whether the lung re-expands.
Drain slowly, generally not more than about 1.5 litres in one sitting, and stop for chest tightness or persistent cough, because of re-expansion pulmonary oedema.
Analgesia, oxygen where hypoxaemic, and treatment of the underlying condition run alongside all of these.
pitfalls: Draining a bilateral transudate in obvious heart failure instead of treating the heart failure.
Treating an empyema with antibiotics alone. It is a drainage problem.
Draining too much too quickly and precipitating re-expansion pulmonary oedema.
Performing pleurodesis when the lung cannot re-expand, which will fail.

probes.q: How is an empyema managed?
probes.a: Chest tube drainage plus antibiotics.

probes.q: Why drain a large effusion slowly?
probes.a: To avoid re-expansion pulmonary oedema. Stop for chest tightness or persistent cough.

probes.q: A recurrent malignant effusion keeps returning after aspiration. What are the definitive options?
probes.a: Pleurodesis or an indwelling pleural catheter, chosen with the patient and depending on whether the lung re-expands after drainage. Pleurodesis fails in a trapped lung.

skill.tx.effusion.dosingNote: Classes, volumes and principles only. Antibiotic choice, antituberculosis regimens and drainage protocols must follow your current national or institutional guideline. CliniX does not prescribe.

cases.title: A laborer with three weeks of breathlessness and evening fever
cases.opening: Deepak Sharma, 28, has walked into the outpatient department, breathless after climbing the stairs. He looks thin and unwell. Introduce yourself and take a history.
cases.fallback: I am not sure what you mean, doctor. Can you ask that a different way?

patient.name: Deepak Sharma
patient.residence: Urban, lives in a rented single room with three co-workers

presenting.reply: Doctor, since about three weeks I have been getting more and more breathless, and there is a dull ache on my right side of the chest.

onset_course.reply: It started slowly, maybe three weeks back, just a mild discomfort. It has been getting steadily worse since then, not sudden at all.

breathlessness_grade.reply: Two weeks ago I could still do my work, lifting bricks. Now I get breathless just walking to the market.

chest_discomfort.reply: It's a dull, heavy ache on the right side, not sharp like a stitch. It doesn't change much with breathing now, though it did in the first week.

orthopnea.reply: I sleep sitting up a bit these days, two pillows, but I don't wake up gasping.

cues: how long have you had the cough
cough.reply: Yes, a dry cough on and off for the same three weeks, nothing comes up with it.

haemoptysis.reply: No, never any blood in what little I cough up.

fever_pattern.reply: I get warm most evenings, feverish by night, and sweat through my clothes some nights. By morning I feel almost normal.

night_sweats.reply: Yes, some nights I have to change my clothes, they get so wet.

weight_appetite.reply: I have lost weight, maybe five kilos in the last month. My appetite has gone down too.

cues: anyone with a chronic cough at home
tb_contact.reply: One of the men I share the room with had a bad cough for months last year, he went to a government clinic for it, I don't know exactly what they said it was.

prior_tb.reply: No, I have never been diagnosed with TB myself before this.

hiv_risk.reply: I have never been tested for HIV. I don't think I have any particular risk for it, but I'm willing to get tested.

cardiac_history.reply: No heart problems that I know of, and my legs are not swollen.

renal_liver_history.reply: No kidney or liver problems, no jaundice ever.

diabetes.reply: No, I've never been told I have diabetes.

smoking_alcohol.reply: I smoke a few bidis a day, maybe five, since I was about twenty. I drink occasionally, nothing heavy.

living_conditions.reply: Four of us share one small room, it doesn't have much of a window.

family_history.reply: Nobody in my family back in the village has had anything like this that I know of.

trauma.reply: No injury to the chest, nothing like that.

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Thin, wasted appearance with visible loss of muscle bulk. Mildly breathless at rest, comfortable sitting upright.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Respiratory rate 22 per minute. Pulse 96 regular. Blood pressure 110/70. SpO2 95 percent on room air. Temperature 37.8 C.

skill.exam.resp.inspection.finding: Right hemithorax appears fuller and moves less than the left. No scars, no chest wall deformity.

skill.exam.resp.trachea.finding: Trachea shifted slightly away from the right side, towards the left.

skill.exam.resp.expansion.finding: Chest expansion reduced on the right, normal on the left.

skill.exam.resp.percussion.finding: Stony dull over the right lower and mid zones, with the upper border of dullness highest in the axilla. Resonant on the left and over the right upper zone.

skill.exam.resp.auscultation.finding: Breath sounds absent over the area of stony dullness. Bronchial breathing heard just above the fluid level, at the right upper zone.

skill.exam.resp.added_sounds.finding: No wheeze. No pleural rub now, though he reports a catching pain in the first week that has since eased as the fluid has increased.

skill.exam.resp.vocal_resonance.finding: Vocal resonance reduced to absent over the dull area. Normal on the left.

cxr.label: Chest radiograph
cxr.result: Right-sided homogeneous opacity with a meniscus obscuring the costophrenic angle, rising towards the axilla. Mild shift of the trachea and mediastinum away from the right. No cavity, no obvious mass.
cxr.note: Confirms there is fluid and roughly how much. It does not say why the fluid is there, that is the next step.

usg_chest.label: Pleural ultrasound
usg_chest.result: Free-flowing, mildly complex effusion, moderate volume, no loculation, no obvious pleural nodularity. Safe aspiration site marked.
usg_chest.note: Confirms fluid, estimates volume, and marks a safe site. A blind tap on the plain film alone is never acceptable.

pleural_tap.label: Diagnostic pleural aspiration
pleural_tap.result: Straw-coloured fluid. Protein 4.8 g/dL. LDH 320 U/L. Glucose 68 mg/dL. Cell count 1,200 cells/mm3, 88 percent lymphocytes. Adenosine deaminase 62 U/L. AFB smear negative. Cytology negative for malignant cells.
pleural_tap.note: This is the test that actually answers the question. A lymphocytic exudate with a markedly raised ADA points strongly to tuberculosis, even with a negative smear, since a TB effusion is typically paucibacillary.

serum_pl.label: Simultaneous serum protein and LDH
serum_pl.result: Serum protein 6.5 g/dL, giving a pleural-to-serum protein ratio of 0.74. Serum LDH 210 U/L, giving a pleural-to-serum LDH ratio of 1.5.
serum_pl.note: Sent at the same time as the tap. Without a paired serum sample, Light's criteria cannot be applied at all, and both ratios here confirm an exudate.

sputum_afb.label: Sputum for acid-fast bacilli
sputum_afb.note: Worth sending even though the diseased compartment here is the pleura, not the lung parenchyma. A negative sputum does not argue against the pleural diagnosis.

hiv.label: HIV test
hiv.note: Sent as a routine part of any newly diagnosed TB, since HIV is the single strongest risk factor for reactivation and would change how closely he needs to be followed.

cect_thorax.label: Contrast-enhanced CT thorax
cect_thorax.result: Right pleural effusion with mild pleural thickening. No discrete mass. Underlying lung parenchyma unremarkable.
cect_thorax.note: Not needed as a first step in a young man with a lymphocytic, ADA-high exudate. CT with pleural biopsy is reserved for when the fluid analysis is inconclusive or malignancy remains suspected, not ordered as a routine reflex alongside the tap.

tumor_markers.label: Tumor marker panel, CEA and CA-125
tumor_markers.result: CEA 3.1 ng/mL, CA-125 mildly raised at 48 U/mL.
tumor_markers.note: Non-specific: both rise with any pleural inflammation, including tuberculosis, and do not distinguish it from malignancy. A marker panel here added nothing that the fluid analysis had not already answered.

echo.label: Echocardiogram
echo.result: Normal biventricular function. No evidence of pulmonary hypertension.
echo.note: A unilateral exudative effusion in a young man with no cardiac history, no orthopnoea and no bilateral or basal-predominant pattern was never suggestive of heart failure. Ordered out of habit rather than a hypothesis.

differentialModel.answer: Right-sided pleural effusion, most likely tuberculous, given the lymphocytic exudate and markedly raised ADA in a young adult with a TB contact and constitutional symptoms. Consider malignancy and a parapneumonic effusion, and, less likely here, a transudative cause such as heart failure.

diagnosis.answer: Tuberculous pleural effusion, right side, exudative and lymphocyte-predominant with a raised ADA, pending microbiological confirmation.

managementModel.answer: Standard antituberculosis therapy under the national programme, notification and contact tracing, therapeutic aspiration only for symptomatic relief or a large effusion rather than routine complete drainage, and follow-up to confirm resolution and watch for residual pleural thickening.

teachingPoints: The trachea was pulled slightly away from the effusion, not towards it. Away means fluid pushing the mediastinum; towards would mean collapse or a fibrothorax instead, a completely different diagnosis.
Reduced vocal resonance over stony dullness is what keeps this on the pleural side of the differential. Increased resonance over the same dullness would mean consolidation, not fluid.
Light's criteria needed a same-day paired serum sample. Sending pleural fluid without it would have made the criteria unusable, no matter how good the pleural result looked.

A negative sputum AFB did not clear tuberculosis here, because the diseased compartment is the pleura, not the lung. A TB effusion is classically paucibacillary and often smear-negative even when the diagnosis is correct.
Lymphocyte predominance and a markedly raised ADA carried more diagnostic weight here than any imaging test ordered afterward.

No clubbing, no long-standing productive cough, and no cardiac findings: absent findings that steer away from bronchiectasis and heart failure respectively, without needing to disprove either formally.
A CT, a tumor marker panel and an echocardiogram were all reasonable-sounding tests that added nothing once the tap itself had already answered the question. A panel is not a plan.
